text: Every circuit run so far has used a perfectly noiseless simulator — the only source of error has been statistical sampling. Real quantum hardware has a second, independent source of error on top of that: the gates themselves aren't perfect. qiskit_aer.noise lets you model that before you ever touch real hardware.

Depolarizing_error of 0.01 and 2 builds a depolarizing error channel for a 2-qubit gate at 1% probability. add_all_qubit_quantum_error attaches that error to every CX gate in the circuit. Pass the noise model into AerSimulator, and every subsequent run applies this error automatically, with no change needed to the circuit itself.

A depolarizing error with probability p works like this: with probability 1 minus p, the gate behaves exactly as intended. With probability p, the gate's output is instead replaced with a fully random, maximally mixed result — as if the correct operation never happened and the qubits' state was scrambled instead. The practical intuition: p is the probability that this particular gate just failed, and when it fails, you get garbage, not a slightly-wrong answer.

Take the familiar Bell-state circuit, but give the CX gate a 1% depolarizing error. The exact math gives P(00) and P(11) at 0.4975 each, barely moved from the noiseless 0.5. But 01 and 10, which were exactly impossible in the noiseless circuit, now sit at 0.0025 each — small, but genuinely nonzero. This is the pattern to watch for diagnostically: noise doesn't just blur existing outcomes, it can open up outcomes the ideal circuit's logic says should never occur at all.

Running this exact noisy circuit at 4096 shots gives something like 00: 2090, 01: 11, 10: 8, 11: 1987. The 01 and 10 counts are small, consistent with their expected count of roughly 10.24 each, but they are not zero — exactly the signature the exact calculation predicted.

Chapter 3 closes with a lab that puts all three versions of this same circuit side by side — exact, noiseless-sampled, and noisy-sampled — and builds the diagnostic habit of telling real noise apart from ordinary sampling noise.
